parts.setUp: Now sort. Each thing goes in the corner that matches what it can do. The Not-sure corner is only a resting place until you check a clue again.
parts.predictQ: Where does the seed belong?
parts.takeaway: Sort things by what they can do, not just by how they look.

challenge.q: A puddle moves when it is windy. Is the puddle living?
challenge.answer: No. The wind pushes it. It does not grow or need food.
mixups: Yes. A puddle moves along the ground, so it must be living.
Yes. A puddle is wet, so it must be living.
Yes. A puddle is outside, so it must be living.
challenge.why: Moving is not enough. A living thing moves by itself, grows and needs air, water and food. A puddle does none of these.

challenge.q: A seed sits still on the shelf. Is it living?
challenge.answer: Yes. It can grow into a plant.
mixups: No. It does not move, so it is non-living.
No. It is small, so it is non-living.
No. It is brown, so it is non-living.
challenge.why: A seed looks still, but it can grow into a plant. Growing is a clue for a living thing.

challenge.q: A bicycle moves when someone pedals it. Is it living?
challenge.answer: No. It cannot move by itself. It does not grow.
mixups: Yes. It moves, so it is living.
Yes. It has a bell and two wheels, so it is living.
No. It is made of metal, and metal things cannot move.
challenge.why: The bicycle only moves because someone pedals it. It does not grow and does not need air, water or food.

challenge.q: A cat is fast asleep and not moving. Is it still living?
challenge.answer: Yes. It still needs air, water and food.
mixups: No. It is not moving, so it is not living now.
Yes. It is soft, so it is living.
Yes. It has fur, so it is living.
challenge.why: A sleeping cat is still living. It still breathes, needs water and food, and can grow.

challenge.q: What do all living things need?
challenge.why: Every living thing needs air, water and food. Living things can also grow, respond and make new living things like themselves.

scriptCautions: The lab's big idea lists the needs, growing and making new living things, but leaves out "respond to changes". When a video states what living things can do, use the book's full set (need water, food and air; grow, respond to changes and reproduce). Lab 1.3 has all six clues.

challenge.q: The toy boat floats on water. Does it need water to live?
challenge.answer: No. It floats on water but does not use it.
mixups: Yes. It floats on the pond all day, so it must need water.
Yes. It gets wet, so it must need water.
challenge.why: Floating on water is not the same as needing it. The boat is non-living. It does not need water, food or air.

challenge.q: What does the bean plant need to stay alive and grow?
challenge.why: The bean plant is living. It needs water, food and air to stay alive and grow.

challenge.q: A toy boat moves across a pond when the wind blows. Is it living?
challenge.answer: No. The wind pushes it. It does not need food.
mixups: Yes. It moves across the pond, so it is living.
Yes. It is on the water, so it is living.
challenge.why: Moving in the wind is not a clue for living. A living thing needs water, food and air, and can grow.

challenge.q: Why does a bean plant need air?
challenge.answer: Living things need air to stay alive.
mixups: Air makes the plant float on water.
Air keeps its leaves dry in the rain.
challenge.why: All living things need air. The bean plant used the air it was given.

challenge.q: Which of these needs water, food and air?
challenge.why: A kitten is living, so it needs water, food and air. The boat, the stone and the kite are non-living.

scriptCautions: The bench offers the bean plant a "food" tray. Keep the lab's own line "A plant makes its own food" in any narration, so pupils do not think plants are fed.

challenge.q: A toy chick moves when it is wound up. Is it living?
challenge.answer: No. It moves, but it does not need food or air.
mixups: Yes. It moves when it is wound up, so it is living.
Yes. It looks like a baby chick, so it is living.
Yes. It makes a sound, so it is living.
challenge.why: One clue is not enough. A living thing shows all six clues. A wound-up toy shows only movement.

challenge.q: How many of the six clues does a living thing show?
challenge.why: The hen showed all six clues. The lamp showed none. Living things show all six.

challenge.q: A kite flies high in the wind. Is it living?
challenge.answer: No. The wind moves it. It does not need food.
mixups: Yes. It flies high in the sky, so it is living.
Yes. It is up in the air, so it must need air.
Yes. It is colourful, so it is living.
challenge.why: A kite only moves because the wind pushes it. It shows none of the six clues.

challenge.q: Which clue shows that a goldfish is living?
mixups: It is orange with shiny scales.
It lives in a bowl on a shelf.
It is small and fits in a hand.
challenge.why: Eating, growing, needing water and air, responding and making young ones are the clues. Colour and size are not.

challenge.q: What does "respond" mean for a living thing?
challenge.answer: It reacts to a change around it.
mixups: It gives out light in a dark room.
It floats on a pond in the sun.
It is heavy and hard to lift.
challenge.why: Living things respond to changes around them. The hen moved when something changed. The lamp did not.

scriptCautions: The six clues are water, food, air, grow, respond and young ones. In exam wording, say "reproduce" as the book does.

challenge.q: A hibiscus has no flower open today. Which group is it in?
challenge.answer: Flowering. It can make a flower.
mixups: Non-flowering, because no flower is open now.
challenge.why: A flowering plant does not always have a flower open. It still belongs to the flowering group.

challenge.q: A tall plant can never make a flower. Which group is it in?
mixups: Flowering, because it has leaves and roots.
challenge.why: Only one thing decides the group: can it make a flower? Height, leaves and roots do not.

challenge.q: A short spiky plant has spore bags under its leaves. Which group is it in?
mixups: Flowering, because it is short and small.
challenge.why: Spore bags are the clue. Plants with spores do not make flowers. Being spiky is not the rule.

challenge.q: What do flowering plants use to make seeds?
challenge.why: Flowering plants make seeds inside a flower.

challenge.q: What do non-flowering plants like ferns use to reproduce?
challenge.why: Non-flowering plants make spores instead of flowers.

scriptCautions: The lab's big idea says flowering plants "make seeds inside a flower". The book says the flowers develop into fruits and the seeds are inside the fruits: use the book's wording. Non-flowering plants reproduce from spores, found in spore bags.

challenge.q: An animal with eight legs sits on a web. Is it an insect?
challenge.answer: No. An insect has six legs. This is a spider.
mixups: Yes. It is small and has a hard body, so it is an insect.
Yes. It has no fur, so it is an insect.
Yes. It sits on a web in the garden, so it is an insect.
challenge.why: Count the legs. An insect has six legs and a hard case. Eight legs is a spider.

challenge.q: A furry animal swims and feeds its young with milk. What is it?
challenge.answer: A mammal, because it has fur and milk.
mixups: A fish, because it swims and lives in water.
A fish, because it swims and has no legs.
An amphibian, because it swims in ponds.
challenge.why: Living in water does not always mean fish. Fur and feeding young with milk are mammal clues.

challenge.q: A feathered animal cannot fly. Is it a bird?
mixups: No. It cannot fly high in the sky, so it is not a bird.
No. It walks on land on two legs, so it is a reptile.
No. Only flying animals are birds.
challenge.why: Feathers, not flight, decide the group. A bird that cannot fly is still a bird.

challenge.q: An animal has moist skin and lays its eggs in water. What is it?
mixups: A fish, because it lives in water.
A reptile, because it has four legs.
A mammal, because it has skin.
challenge.why: Moist skin and eggs laid in water are the amphibian clues, like the frog.

challenge.q: How many legs does an insect have?
mixups: Any number, if it is small.
challenge.why: An insect has six legs and a hard case. Eight legs is a spider.

scriptCautions: The bench sorts by covering ("wet scales", "dry scales", "hard case"). For the exam, use the book's features: fish have scales, fins and gills; reptiles have dry, scaly skin; insects have six legs, one pair of feelers and three body parts (head, thorax, abdomen). The book says MOST mammals give birth to live young.

challenge.q: Why do we need a microscope to see bacteria?
challenge.answer: They are too tiny to see with our eyes.
mixups: They move too fast for our eyes to follow.
They only come out at night when it is dark.
challenge.why: Bacteria are tiny living things. Only a microscope makes them big enough to see.

challenge.q: Does a mushroom make its own food?
challenge.answer: No. It soaks up food from around it.
mixups: Yes, it makes food in its cap, like a plant.
Only in the dark, under the soil.
Only when it rains for a whole day.
challenge.why: A mushroom is a fungus, not a plant. Fungi cannot make their own food.

challenge.q: Do all bacteria make us unwell?
challenge.answer: No. Some bacteria help us, like in yoghurt.
mixups: Yes, all bacteria are harmful and make us ill.
No, only fungi can make us unwell.
Yes, every germ is bad for our bodies.
challenge.why: Some bacteria help us. Some can make us unwell.

challenge.q: Which of these is a fungus?
mixups: A bean plant in a pot.
challenge.why: Yeast is a fungus. Mushrooms and bread mould are fungi too.

challenge.q: Is the mould on old bread alive?
challenge.answer: Yes. Mould is a living fungus.
mixups: No, it is just a dark stain on the bread.
No, it only grows on plastic and stones.
No, it is only dust that fell on it.
challenge.why: Mould is a fungus. It is living: it grows and spreads over the bread.

scriptCautions: Book: there are four groups of living things (plants, animals, fungi, bacteria). Fungi do not make their own food and reproduce by spores. Bacteria can be rod-shaped, round or spiral-shaped. Give one useful and one harmful example of each.

challenge.q: Why do we improve an object?
mixups: To make it look different and colourful
To use up more of the materials
To make it heavier to carry around
challenge.why: We change a material so the object does its job better.

challenge.q: A paper strap tore easily. What is a good replacement?
challenge.answer: Fabric, because it bends and is strong
mixups: Glass, because it is hard and see-through
Another paper strap, but a thicker one
Paper towel, because it is soft and thick

challenge.q: Does any new material always make an object better?

Only if it is made of metal or glass

challenge.q: Which shows an improvement was really tested?

challenge.why: A seed grows into a seedling, and the seedling grows into an adult plant.

challenge.q: What does a seed need to start growing?
challenge.answer: Water, air and the right warmth
mixups: Only strong bright light from the sun
challenge.why: Both seeds started growing, even the one in the dark. A seed needs water, air and warmth to start.

challenge.q: The seedling in the dark box was pale and weak. Why?

challenge.q: Where do a plant's new seeds come from?
challenge.answer: Inside the fruit of the adult plant
mixups: From the roots under the ground

challenge.why: The adult plant grows flowers, then fruit. The new seeds are inside the fruit.

challenge.q: On the windowsill, the sunny seedling grew from 1 cm to 12 cm. What does this show?
challenge.answer: A seedling grows taller over the days
mixups: A seedling stays the same height each day
challenge.why: A seedling grows taller each day when it has water, air and light.

challenge.q: Which animal has three stages: egg, young and adult?
challenge.why: A grasshopper has three stages. A butterfly, a mosquito and a beetle have four, with a pupa.

challenge.q: What happens inside the pupa?
mixups: The animal turns back into an egg
challenge.why: The pupa does not eat. Inside it, the adult is forming.

challenge.q: A frog has three stages. Does the tadpole look like the adult frog?
challenge.answer: No, it has a tail and lives in water
mixups: Yes, it looks exactly the same as the frog
Yes, but it is a lot smaller
challenge.why: Three stages does not mean the young looks like the adult. A tadpole looks nothing like a frog.

challenge.q: A caterpillar is the young of which animal?
challenge.why: A caterpillar hatches from a butterfly egg, becomes a pupa, then an adult butterfly.

challenge.q: The four stages of a mosquito, in order, are
challenge.why: Egg, then larva in the water, then pupa, then the adult flies away.

scriptCautions: The lab's big idea gives the four stages as "egg, young, pupa and adult". The book, and the bench's own Challenge, say egg, larva, pupa, adult. Use "larva".
Name each young one correctly: nymph (grasshopper, cockroach), tadpole (frog), caterpillar (butterfly larva), wriggler (mosquito larva).

challenge.q: Does a magnet attract anything made of metal?
challenge.answer: No. It attracts only some metals, like iron and steel.

challenge.why: Steel is attracted by a magnet, so steel is a magnetic material.

parts.predictQ: To bring the cart to the flag, should the wand attract or repel it?
parts.takeaway: Unlike poles (red and blue) attract and bring the cart. Like poles (red and red, blue and blue) repel and push it away. We choose on purpose.

challenge.q: Why do we choose a magnet's pole on purpose when building a toy?
challenge.answer: To make the toy attract or repel as we planned
mixups: To make the magnet look nicer
So that the toy can use more magnets than before
Because red is the strong end
challenge.why: Which poles face decides attract or repel. We choose it to fit the plan.

challenge.q: Two magnets move apart when they face each other. What poles are facing?
challenge.answer: Like poles, such as red facing red
mixups: Unlike poles, such as red facing blue
challenge.why: Like poles repel. Unlike poles attract.

challenge.q: A toy cart will not move toward the wand. What could improve it?
challenge.answer: Flip a magnet's pole, or move the wand closer
mixups: Paint the cart a new colour
Swap the magnet for a plastic part
Add a much heavier flag at the end of the track
challenge.why: Wrong poles, or too far away. Change one of those and test again.

challenge.q: Why do we test a toy after building it?
challenge.answer: To find out if it really works the way we planned
mixups: Testing is only needed if the toy looks wrong at first
challenge.why: A test shows what really happens. Then we can improve it.

challenge.q: Which of these shows a toy was really improved?
challenge.answer: Comparing how it worked before and after one change
mixups: Saying that it looks a lot better now than it did before
challenge.why: 10 cm, then 25, then 40: the attempts show the change helped.

scriptCautions: Change one thing at a time, then compare before and after (a fair test).
